title: New Testament Survey I: Gospels and Acts
summary: The world of the New Testament, the four Gospels' portraits of Jesus, and the spread of the church in Acts.
description: This course introduces the setting of the New Testament and surveys the four Gospels and the Acts of the Apostles. It explains why there are four Gospels, what each one emphasises, the main events of Jesus' life, death and resurrection, and how the gospel spread from Jerusalem to Rome by the power of the Holy Spirit.
objectives: Describe the political and religious world into which Jesus came
Explain the purpose and emphasis of each Gospel
Outline the main events of the life of Christ
Trace the expansion of the church in Acts
outcomes: Name the groups and powers of first-century Judea
Compare Matthew, Mark, Luke and John
Place the main events of Jesus' ministry, death and resurrection in order
Explain the significance of Pentecost and the Jerusalem council

modules.title: The World of the New Testament
modules.intro: Before reading the Gospels, we meet the world Jesus entered: Rome, the Jews, the temple and the synagogue.

lessons.title: Rome and the Herods
lessons.body:
When Jesus was born, Judea was under the Roman Empire. Caesar Augustus ordered the census that brought Joseph and Mary to Bethlehem (Luke 2:1-7). Herod the Great, a king appointed by Rome, tried to kill the infant Jesus (Matthew 2:16).

Later, Herod Antipas ruled Galilee and beheaded John the Baptist, and Pontius Pilate governed Judea (Luke 3:1).

Roman roads, peace and the common Greek language helped the gospel spread quickly (Galatians 4:4).

lessons.title: Jewish groups and leaders
lessons.body:
Several groups appear in the Gospels:

- **Pharisees:** strict keepers of the law and their traditions; often in conflict with Jesus (Matthew 23).
- **Sadducees:** priestly aristocrats who denied the resurrection (Acts 23:8).
- **Scribes:** experts in the law.
- **Zealots:** nationalists seeking to overthrow Rome; Simon the disciple was one (Luke 6:15).
- **The Sanhedrin:** the Jewish ruling council led by the high priest.

Many ordinary Jews were waiting for "the consolation of Israel" (Luke 2:25).

lessons.title: Temple, synagogue and Messiah
lessons.body:
The **temple** in Jerusalem, rebuilt by Herod, was the centre of sacrifice and the great feasts. The **synagogue** was the local place of prayer and Scripture reading; Jesus taught in synagogues (Luke 4:16-21).

The Jews expected a **Messiah** (Greek: *Christ*, "Anointed One"). Many hoped for a political king to drive out Rome. Jesus came as King, but first as the suffering Servant who would give His life a ransom for many (Mark 10:45).

The Gospels show how He fulfilled the Scriptures in ways that surprised even His disciples.

Pharisees, Sadducees, scribes and the Sanhedrin shaped Jewish life.

modules.title: Matthew and Mark
modules.intro: Matthew presents Jesus as the promised King of the Jews; Mark presents Him as the active, suffering Servant.

lessons.title: Why four Gospels?
lessons.body:
The four Gospels are four inspired portraits of one Lord. Matthew, Mark and Luke are called the **Synoptic** Gospels ("seen together") because they share much material and order. John is different, adding much not found elsewhere.

Each writer selected and arranged events for his readers and purpose (John 20:30-31). Differences of detail are like witnesses describing the same event from different places; they strengthen rather than weaken the testimony.

Together they give a full picture: King, Servant, Son of man and Son of God.

lessons.title: Matthew: the King and His kingdom
lessons.body:
Matthew, a tax collector turned apostle, wrote especially for Jewish readers. He begins with Jesus' genealogy from Abraham and David (Matthew 1:1) and often says, "that it might be fulfilled" (Matthew 1:22).

He groups Jesus' teaching into five great discourses, including the Sermon on the Mount (chapters 5-7), and speaks of "the kingdom of heaven".

Matthew ends with the Great Commission: "Go ye therefore, and teach all nations" (Matthew 28:19-20). The King of the Jews is Lord of all nations.

lessons.title: Mark: the Servant in action
lessons.body:
Mark, linked by early tradition with Peter, is the shortest Gospel and probably written for Roman readers. It moves quickly; the word "straightway" (immediately) appears again and again.

Mark focuses on what Jesus did: healing, casting out demons, calming storms. Its key verse is Mark 10:45: the Son of man came "not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many".

Nearly a third of Mark covers the last week of Jesus' life. At the cross a Roman centurion confesses, "Truly this man was the Son of God" (Mark 15:39).

terms.def: 'Good news'; also one of the four books about Jesus' life.

Matthew presents Jesus as the promised King who fulfils Scripture.

Differences of detail are like faithful witnesses from different angles.

modules.title: Luke and John
modules.intro: Luke presents Jesus as the Saviour of all people; John presents Him as the eternal Son of God.

lessons.title: Luke: the Saviour of the lost
lessons.body:
Luke, a physician and companion of Paul, wrote an "orderly" account for Theophilus after careful investigation (Luke 1:1-4). He gives the fullest birth narrative and many parables found only in Luke, such as the Good Samaritan and the Prodigal Son (Luke 10; 15).

Luke highlights Jesus' care for the poor, women, Samaritans and outcasts, and the work of the Holy Spirit and prayer.

Its key verse: "the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost" (Luke 19:10). Luke wrote Acts as volume two.

lessons.title: John: believe and live
lessons.body:
John, "the disciple whom Jesus loved", wrote last, perhaps around AD 90. He opens in eternity: "In the beginning was the Word... and the Word was God... And the Word was made flesh" (John 1:1, 14).

John records seven signs (miracles), such as water into wine and the raising of Lazarus, and seven "I am" sayings: the bread of life, the light of the world, the door, the good shepherd, the resurrection and the life, the way, the truth and the life, and the true vine.

His purpose: "that ye might believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God; and that believing ye might have life through his name" (John 20:31).

lessons.title: The ministry of Jesus
lessons.body:
Jesus' public ministry lasted about three years. It began with His baptism by John and the temptation in the wilderness (Matthew 3-4).

In Galilee He called disciples, preached the kingdom, healed the sick and taught in parables. He chose twelve apostles (Mark 3:14). At Caesarea Philippi, Peter confessed, "Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God" (Matthew 16:16). From then Jesus began to teach that He must suffer, die and rise again (16:21).

He then "stedfastly set his face to go to Jerusalem" (Luke 9:51).

modules.title: The Cross and the Empty Tomb
modules.intro: All four Gospels slow down for the final week. This week follows Jesus from the triumphal entry to the resurrection appearances.

lessons.title: The final week
lessons.body:
Jesus entered Jerusalem on a donkey, fulfilling Zechariah 9:9, as crowds cried "Hosanna" (Matthew 21:1-11). He cleansed the temple and taught in its courts.

At the Passover meal with His disciples He washed their feet and instituted the Lord's Supper: "this is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many for the remission of sins" (Matthew 26:28).

In Gethsemane He prayed, "not my will, but thine, be done" (Luke 22:42). Judas betrayed Him, and He was arrested and tried before the Sanhedrin, Pilate and Herod.

lessons.title: The crucifixion
lessons.body:
Pilate, knowing Jesus was innocent, gave Him to be crucified. Jesus was crucified between two thieves at Golgotha. The Gospels record seven sayings from the cross, including "Father, forgive them" (Luke 23:34), "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" (Matthew 27:46) and "It is finished" (John 19:30).

Darkness covered the land, the veil of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom (Matthew 27:51), showing the way into God's presence was opened.

Jesus truly died and was buried in Joseph of Arimathea's tomb.

lessons.title: He is risen
lessons.body:
On the first day of the week, women found the tomb empty. Angels said, "He is not here: for he is risen, as he said" (Matthew 28:6).

Jesus appeared to Mary Magdalene, to two disciples on the Emmaus road, to the apostles, to Thomas, and to more than five hundred at once (1 Corinthians 15:5-8). He showed His hands and side and ate with them (Luke 24:39-43).

After forty days He ascended to heaven from the Mount of Olives, promising the Holy Spirit and His return (Acts 1:3-11).

modules.title: Acts: The Gospel Goes Out
modules.intro: Luke's second volume shows the risen Christ, by His Spirit, spreading the gospel from Jerusalem to Rome.

lessons.title: Jerusalem and Pentecost
lessons.body:
Acts 1:8 outlines the book: "ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth."

On the day of Pentecost the Holy Spirit came upon the disciples, and they spoke in other tongues (Acts 2:4). Peter preached Christ crucified and risen, calling, "Repent, and be baptized" (2:38); about three thousand were added.

The early church devoted itself to the apostles' doctrine, fellowship, breaking of bread and prayers (2:42), and endured persecution, including the martyrdom of Stephen (Acts 7).

lessons.title: Judea, Samaria and the Gentiles
lessons.body:
Persecution scattered believers, and the gospel went to Samaria through Philip (Acts 8). Saul of Tarsus, a persecutor, met the risen Christ on the Damascus road and became Paul, apostle to the Gentiles (Acts 9).

God sent Peter to the Roman centurion Cornelius, and the Spirit fell on Gentiles as He had on the Jews (Acts 10:44-48).

The Jerusalem council (Acts 15) decided that Gentiles are saved by grace through faith, without becoming Jews through circumcision (15:11).

lessons.title: To the ends of the earth
lessons.body:
From Antioch, Paul and Barnabas were sent on the first missionary journey (Acts 13:2-3). Paul made three journeys, planting churches across Asia Minor and Greece: Philippi, Thessalonica, Corinth, Ephesus.

Arrested in Jerusalem, Paul appealed to Caesar and was taken to Rome, surviving a shipwreck on the way (Acts 27).

Acts ends with Paul in Rome under house arrest, "preaching the kingdom of God... with all confidence, no man forbidding him" (Acts 28:31). The story is unfinished; it continues through every generation of witnesses, including ours.

short.model: They are four inspired portraits of the one Christ, each written for particular readers and purposes, giving a fuller picture together.

short.q: What is the purpose of John's Gospel, according to John 20:31?
short.model: That readers might believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and believing have life through His name.

short.q: What did the tearing of the temple veil signify?
short.model: That through Christ's death the way into God's presence was opened for sinners.

short.q: Give three pieces of evidence for the resurrection from the Gospels and Paul.
short.model: The empty tomb, the many appearances (including to over five hundred at once), and His bodily presence: showing His hands and side and eating with the disciples.
The Holy Spirit came upon the disciples, who spoke in other tongues; Peter preached Christ and about three thousand were saved and baptized.

short.q: Why was the Jerusalem council (Acts 15) important?
short.model: It confirmed that Gentiles are saved by grace through faith, without needing circumcision or becoming Jews.

assignments.title: One Christ, four portraits
assignments.prompt: Choose one event recorded in at least three Gospels (for example the feeding of the five thousand or the resurrection morning). Compare the accounts, note what each adds, and explain how the differences fit together and serve each writer's purpose.

assignments.title: Witnesses today
assignments.prompt: Using Acts 1:8 and two events from Acts, explain what it means for a believer and a local church in Nigeria to be Christ's witnesses today. Include one practical step you will take.
